full_judgment:
2. The pre-emptor filed an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to pre-empt a transfer date 13.11.76. He obtained a copy of the impaired kabala dated 27.2.77 and came to know of the transfer. Thereafter he filed the instant application for pre-emption on 29.3.77. Thereafter the objection was filed by the pre-emptee on 5.11.77 challenging the pre-emption, contending, inter alia, the maintainability of the application itself. According to the pre-emptee the application for pre-emption was premature since the formalities under section 60 of the Registration Act was not then complete. There after an application was filed by the pre-emptee on 3.4.78 under Order 7, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting the petition for pre-emption. In such circumstances the pre-emptor filed an application before the learned Subordinate Judge for an adjournment on the ground that a similar question was awaiting decision by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. The learned Subordinate Judge rejected the petition and fixed the matter for orders on 7.9.78. On the said date the learned Subordinate Judge took the view in accordance with the earlier decisions relating on the point and held that unless the registration was complete, the right of pre-emption does not accrue and as such the instant application for pre-emption was premature. Accordingly Miscellaneous case was rejected evidently under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. 

 4. Mr. Khademul Islam Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the opposite parties has strenuously argued that there is no error on the face of the record and the order of the learned Subordinate Judge was not vitiated by any such error. According to Mr. Islam Chowdhury the impugned order was perfectly in accordance with law as it then was. The learned Subordinate Judge relied upon certain decisions which completely covered the field Therefore there was no error in the decision of the learned Subordinate Judge. As regards the immaturity of the petition for pre-emption, Mr. Islam has pointed out that in the written objection filed by the pre-emptee it was specifically stated that the application for pre-emption was premature in the absence of the registration of the impugned document according to law. Therefore, the learned Subordinate Judge had ample jurisdiction to entertain a petition under Order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and to knock out the pre-emptor on the ground that the pre-emption was premature. Mr. Khademul Islam has also relief upon the decision referred to above by Mr. Shamsuddin Ahmed and sought to distinguish it by explaining that pendency of the proceeding before the Court of origin. He has also drawn our attention that the rectification was available at any time before the pronouncement of the judgment. According to him, the judgment was pronounced by the learned Subordinate Judge on 7.9.78. It is evident from the dates noted above that registration was not complete on the date of the judgment i.e. on 7.9.78, Registration was made on 12.4.79 when the matter was not pending before trial Court but it was pending before this Court. Mr. Islam Chowdhury wants to put a narrow interpretation of the expression pendency of the proceeding. In our opinion, such interpretation does not follow from the language Used by their. Lordships of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh in the case relied upon by both the learned Advocates. In our opinion; the pendency of the proceeding has a wider connotation, it means pending before a competent Court and awaiting final decision in the matter. Therefore, we are not inclined to accept the narrow and restricted interpretation of the decision in the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Mokhles Ali as referred to above. 

 6. Although there is no error apparent on the face of the record in so far as the impugned order is concerned yet in view of the change in the law or rather interpretation of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as made by their Lordships of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court in the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Mokles Ali referred to above, all Courts subordinate to the Appellate Division are bound by such decision and the principles laid down therein. In respectful obedience to the view expressed in the aforesaid decision, we hold that the application for pre-emption is no longer premature since the defect has been cured during the pendency of the matter and as such the pre-emptor's case must be remitted to the learned Subordinate Judge for disposal according to law and in the light of the observation made above. The parties as required in law are to adduce evidence in support of their respective claims before the learned Subordinate Judge who is directed to dispose of the matter within six months from date.
